blocks.text: Chapter 5.
Regression to the Mean and Taming Predictions

Fifth night, friend — and it opens with a confrontation. A young Daniel Kahneman is lecturing Israeli air force flight instructors on the science of training: reward works better than punishment. A seasoned officer stands up, annoyed, and tells him flatly that the science is backwards.

"Many times," the officer says, in effect, "I've praised a cadet for a beautifully executed maneuver — and the next time, he flies worse. And I've screamed at a cadet for a botched one — and the next time, he flies better. So don't tell me reward works and punishment doesn't." The room nodded, friend. The officer's experience was real. His data were accurate.
And Kahneman, standing there, had what he later called one of the most satisfying eureka experiences of my career — because the officer was right about every fact and wrong about the cause.

Pause and guess: The praised cadets really did fly worse the next time. The screamed-at cadets really did improve. And yet the praise ruined nothing and the screaming fixed nothing. What was ACTUALLY happening?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Regression to the mean, friend — luck evening out. Every single maneuver is skill plus a big dose of random variation. A cadet gets praised only after an unusually good attempt — which means he was flying above his own average, so his next attempt will almost certainly be closer to that average: worse, praise or no praise. A cadet gets screamed at only after an unusually bad one — below his own average, due to bounce back, screaming or silence. The instructor had attached a causal story — his own feedback — to fluctuations that needed no cause at all. Kahneman proved it with a chalk circle and some coins: officers tossed coins at a target twice, no feedback anywhere; those who did well on throw one mostly did worse on throw two, and vice versa — regression, with nobody praising or blaming anyone. And now the dark, magnificent implication, friend, maybe the saddest sentence in this whole book: the world's feedback is rigged against kindness. We naturally punish after bad performances and reward after good ones — and performance then drifts back to normal either way — so life itself statistically guarantees that harshness feels effective and generosity feels like it backfired. Whole philosophies of parenting, coaching, and management were built on an arithmetic artifact.
A little talent, a lot of luck

Kahneman compresses the whole idea into two lines, friend — write them somewhere: success = talent + luck. Great success = a little more talent + a LOT of luck. Any performance extreme enough to catch your eye almost certainly carried an outsized helping of luck — and luck, by definition, doesn't repeat.

Watch it work. Two golfers on day one of a tournament: one shoots a brilliant 66, the other a miserable 77. Best forecast for day two? Both drift toward the field's average — the leader scores worse, the straggler better — no pressure, no choking, no fire in the belly. Just yesterday's luck failing to show up twice. The famous Sports Illustrated jinx — athletes slumping right after making the cover — dissolves the same way: you only make the cover after a stretch when luck ran scorching hot; what follows is ordinary, and the pundits blame swollen ego or media pressure. The ski-jump commentator murmuring that the leader's weaker second jump shows he's "tense, protecting his lead"? Narrating arithmetic, friend, in the costume of psychology.

And it hides in the strangest places. Highly intelligent women tend to marry men less intelligent than themselves. Dinner parties will offer you theories — intimidation, preference, fear. The real explanation needs no psychology at all: whenever the correlation between spouses is imperfect — and it is — extreme scorers on one side pair, on average, with less extreme scorers on the other. Correlation less than one guarantees regression — Galton discovered it in the 1880s in the heights of parents and children, and it took the best statisticians of the age years to believe it. Correlation and regression aren't two phenomena, friend; they're one fact seen from two windows. That's also why credible science demands control groups: give depressed children an energy drink for three months and they will improve — because an extreme group drifts toward the mean no matter what you pour in the glass. Only improvement beyond the control group's counts.

Pause and guess: Now for the fix. Julie is a university senior. She read fluently at age FOUR. Quick, from the gut: what's her GPA? Most people say about 3.7. How did your mind produce that number — and what's wrong with it?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Intensity matching, friend — the swap you met two nights ago. "Reading at four" is this impressive, so the forecast becomes an equally impressive GPA: 3.7. But notice what that assumes: that early reading predicts adult grades PERFECTLY — a correlation of 1.0. The real correlation is maybe .30 — most of Julie's GPA is decided by things you know nothing about — so an honest forecast must sit much closer to the plain average. Kahneman's four-step cure, usable on any forecast you'll ever make: (1) Start at the baseline — the average outcome for the reference class (the mean GPA of all seniors; what you'd predict knowing nothing about Julie). (2) Note your intuitive estimate — the 3.7. (3) Honestly estimate the correlation between your evidence and the outcome — here, about .30. (4) Move from the baseline toward your intuition by exactly that proportion — 30 percent of the way, no further. Correlation zero? Stay at the baseline. Correlation one? Trust your gut fully. Everything between — which is everything, friend — gets weighted honestly. The price is real: tamed forecasts never call extremes — they feel gray, timid, unsatisfying. Moderation is the price of accuracy. Keep evaluation and prediction in separate pockets: "this candidate interviewed brilliantly" is a fact about today; "this candidate will perform brilliantly" is a bet about a future the interview barely touches. (One principled exception: the venture capitalist hunting hundred-fold returns may rationally overweight long shots — but as a stated policy with sized stakes, never as a gut feeling in a good suit.)
Before you go

So: extreme performances revert with no cause needed — the flight instructor's data were perfect and his conclusion was upside down; the world's raw feedback is rigged to teach harshness and slander kindness; great success is a little more talent and a lot of luck, which is why covers jinx and shakeups "work"; correlation below one guarantees regression — demand control groups; and tame every forecast with the four steps: baseline, intuition, honest correlation, partial move. This week, friend: before crediting any coaching, treatment, or scolding for an improvement after a bad stretch — ask what the numbers would have done on their own.

Tomorrow night, the giant: overconfidence — the bias Kahneman calls the most damaging of them all. Why did the interviewers assessing soldiers keep total confidence in judgments they knew barely predicted anything? Why do simple checklists and dumb little formulas beat seasoned experts at predicting wine prices, parole violations, and marital happiness? And the single most useful meeting trick in the whole book — the premortem. Next time: illusions, formulas, and the premortem.
Key takeaways
The flight-instructor illusion: praised cadets regress down, scolded cadets regress up — feedback gets credit for what luck was returning anyway.
The world's feedback is statistically rigged against kindness: harshness will always feel effective; don't believe it.
Success = talent + luck; great success = a little more talent + a lot of luck — hence the Sports Illustrated jinx, day-two fades, and post-shakeup "recoveries."
Correlation < 1 guarantees regression (Galton): smart women marrying down is arithmetic, not intimidation — and extreme groups improve without treatment, which is why control groups exist.
Tame predictions in four steps: baseline average → intuitive estimate → honest correlation → move only that fraction from baseline toward intuition.
Moderation is the price of accuracy: tamed forecasts never call extremes — keep "evaluated brilliantly" separate from "will perform brilliantly," and bet long shots only as stated policy.
